title: Make each evidence mark a decision
statement: Make each evidence tap or highlight a decision that can be wrong and is then discussed, steered to the parts that matter, since untrained highlighting is rated low utility.
example: A review rated highlighting and underlining as low utility, one of five techniques so rated.
detail: A Grade 4 lesson's research note cites a review that rates highlighting and underlining as low utility, one of five techniques so rated, with the review's own caveat that most reviewed studies gave participants no training in what to mark, so the finding argues against untrained marking, not against a taught selection routine. It concludes that a tap-the-evidence interaction is not itself the learning: what makes it work is that the tap is a decision that can be wrong and is then argued about. The Grade 9 desktop brief adds a study of 371 students in grades 5–8 in which digital highlighting was linked positively to comprehension and paper highlighting negatively, much of it falling outside the important parts of the text, and asks for highlighting steered to the parts that matter, such as a 'highlight the evidence' task.
against: Digital highlighting was linked positively to comprehension in that study, a link the low-utility rating does not explain, and annotating and dictionary use showed no link (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/edtech-desktop-design.md`, line 100). Most reviewed studies gave no training in what to mark: "Caveat, stated in the monograph's own limitation and repeated in secondary coverage: most reviewed studies gave participants no training in what to mark. So the finding argues against untrained marking, not against a taught selection routine." (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l2-the-cyclops.md`, lines 404-407).

evidence.quote: rate highlighting and underlining as low utility, one of five techniques so rated
So the finding argues against untrained marking, not against a taught selection routine.
What makes it work is that the tap is a decision that can be wrong and is then argued about.
Goodwin et al. (2020, AERJ), 371 students in grades 5–8: students highlighted and annotated less on digital text.
But digital highlighting was linked positively to comprehension, while paper highlighting was linked negatively (much of it fell outside the important parts of the text).
*Implication:* make highlighting effortless and steer it to the parts that matter (for example a "highlight the evidence" task).

**Highlighting on its own does nothing.** Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham, Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1), 2013, rate highlighting and underlining as low utility, one of five techniques so rated, against practice testing and distributed practice as high utility. The reported reason is that most students over-highlight and that highlighters were at a disadvantage on inference questions. [DOI 10.1177/1529100612453266](https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266);
For us it argues one specific thing: a tap-the-evidence interaction is not itself the learning. What makes it work is that the tap is a decision that can be wrong and is then argued about.

Caveat, stated in the monograph's own limitation and repeated in secondary coverage: most reviewed studies gave participants no training in what to mark. So the finding argues against untrained marking, not against a taught selection routine.
